Recommendation.Description: Open the Global Manager UI (System, Location Manager) and check which Global Manager is active. If the active Global Manager is lost, follow the NSX Federation disaster recovery procedure and make the standby active. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/disaster-recovery-using-federation.html

Two Global Managers claim the active role. Do not change global configuration. Decide which Global Manager holds the valid configuration and force the other one to standby, as described in the NSX Federation recovery documentation. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/324244
Check that the Global Manager appliance is powered on and that the cloud proxy can reach it on TCP 443. If its certificate was replaced, update the trusted certificate of the adapter instance.

Deploy a standby Global Manager in another site and add it under System, Location Manager, Add Standby Global Manager. Without a standby the global configuration cannot be changed if the active Global Manager is lost. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/disaster-recovery-using-federation.html

Some NSX API calls of the collection failed, so part of the data is unknown and the alerts that depend on it are not evaluated. Read the property 'NSX API calls without an answer' on the federation object: it lists the manager, the call and the HTTP status. HTTP 403 points to missing rights of the collection account, HTTP 5xx or a timeout to a manager under load or a service that is down.

The collection is close to the limits of the managers or of the collection interval. Lengthen the collection interval of the account, reduce the policies whose rules are collected, or lower 'Managers collected in parallel'. Check the load of the manager named in the NSX alarms.

No Global Manager answered, none is active, or the active one did not return its locations (the property 'Collection mode' says which), so the collection uses the list of locations it cached earlier and collects the Local Managers only. Check the Global Manager addresses of the account and the alert on the Global Managers.
One account monitors one federation. Remove the address named in the property 'Global Managers not collected' from this account and create a second account for the other federation.

A Global Manager that comes back after a failover has no role until it is added again as the standby. In the UI of the active Global Manager, open System, Location Manager and make it the standby. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/disaster-recovery-using-federation.html
Upgrade the Global Manager that is behind. NSX refuses a switchover while the active and the standby Global Manager run different versions. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/449461

Finish the upgrade in the order NSX Federation requires: the standby Global Manager, then the active Global Manager, then the Local Managers. A Local Manager must not run a newer release than the Global Manager. Take a backup of every manager cluster first. A paused upgrade is resumed or cancelled in System, Upgrade. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/435153
The collection of this cycle is partial. Raise 'API call budget per manager and cycle' in the advanced settings of the adapter instance, or lengthen the collection interval.
Open System, Appliances on the manager and check the state of each node and service group. Restore or redeploy the failed node.
Configure a backup target and a schedule under System, Backup and Restore on the manager, then run a backup and confirm that it succeeds. A manager can only be restored from its own backup.

Replace the certificate before it expires (System, Certificates). An expired manager certificate breaks the connection between the Global Manager and the Local Managers. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/429189

Check the network path between the active Global Manager and the Local Manager of this location (TCP 443 and 1236 in both directions) and the state of the Local Manager cluster. The location keeps forwarding traffic with its last configuration.
Check that the cloud proxy can reach the Local Manager on TCP 443 and that the account of the adapter instance is valid on this Local Manager. This is the monitoring path only.

The Local Manager presents a certificate that is not the one the Global Manager holds for it. Confirm the certificate change is expected, then update the location in the Global Manager so the thumbprint matches.
Open the location in System, Location Manager and read the sync status details. Start a full sync again from the Global Manager once the cause (connectivity, version, disk space) is fixed.

Check the RTEP network between the edge clusters of the locations: RTEP VLAN, MTU (1700 recommended), routing between RTEP subnets and the state of the edge nodes. Stretched segments and gateways depend on these sessions.

The location and the Global Manager run different NSX releases (the first three numbers of the version). That is expected only during an upgrade. Complete the upgrade so that all managers run the same release. A different patch level of the same release does not raise this alert.
Check the connectivity between the two managers named on the channel (TCP 443 and 1236) and the state of both manager clusters.
Check the BGP neighbor on the Tier-0 gateway: interface state of the edge uplink, the peer router, AS numbers, passwords and timers.
The session is established but the peer advertises nothing. Check the routing policy and redistribution on the peer router.
Check the RTEP network between the two edge nodes of this tunnel: MTU on the whole path (1700 recommended), packet loss on the physical links and the load of the edge nodes.

Packets on this tunnel are blocked, not lost. Check the firewalls between the RTEP subnets of the two locations (Geneve, UDP 6081), the gateway firewall rules of the edge nodes, and any change made to them around the time the alert started.

The session went down and came back. Check the edge uplink and the peer router logs for interface flaps, hold-timer expiries or BFD events around that time. Repeated flaps usually point to a physical link, an MTU mismatch or a peer under load.

The inter-site BGP session of this tunnel went down and came back. Check the RTEP path between the two edge nodes (physical links, WAN, MTU 1700 on the whole path) and the load of both edges around that time. Repeated flaps on every tunnel of an edge point to the edge or its uplinks; on one tunnel, to the path.

A delta sync from the Global Manager to the location named in the alarm failed. Check the connection between them (TCP 1236 in both directions) and the async-replicator service on both sides (get service async_replicator, log /var/log/async-replicator/ar.log). If the alarm stays after the connection is back, start a full sync of the location from System, Location Manager. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/using-the-gm-and-lm-ui/monitoring-nsx-federation-locations.html

Open System, User Management, LDAP on the manager named in the alarm and check the identity source: the LDAP server answers on its port, its certificate is still the trusted one, and the bind credentials are valid. Local accounts keep working while the source is unreachable.

Measure the round-trip time between the Global Manager and the Local Manager of this location. Broadcom documents 150 ms as the limit between locations that share stretched networks (500 ms otherwise), and the maximum RTT setting of the location (System, Location Manager) is the limit NSX applies. Look for WAN congestion, a path change or a degraded link. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/345822

Open the object in the Global Manager and read the error for each location of its span. Fix the cause (a missing edge cluster, an address conflict, a location that is not reachable), then save the object again.

Check the connectivity between the active and the standby Global Manager (ping, then TCP 443 and 1236) and the state of both Global Manager clusters. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/using-the-gm-and-lm-ui/monitoring-nsx-federation-locations.html

Check the connectivity between the Global Manager and the location (ping, TCP 1236 in both directions) and that the async-replicator service runs on both sides (get service async_replicator). Its log is /var/log/async-replicator/ar.log. See https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/vcf/vcf-9-0-and-later/9-0/advanced-network-management/administration-guide/managing-nsx-t-in-multiple-locations/nsx-t-federation/using-the-gm-and-lm-ui/monitoring-nsx-federation-locations.html

Run get site-replicator remote-sites on the Local Managers to see the connection state between the locations, then check TCP 1236 between them. A location that is connected but not synchronized may still be electing its leader; check again after a few seconds.

Measure the round-trip time between the two managers named in the alarm. Broadcom documents 150 ms as the limit between locations that share stretched networks (500 ms otherwise); look for WAN congestion or a path change. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/345822

The sync queue grows when the remote location cannot keep up or cannot be reached. Check the connectivity to the remote location and /var/log/async-replicator/ar.log. See https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/414606
The location is in an inconsistent state. Delete the onboarding status of the location on the Global Manager, as the NSX alarm describes, then start the configuration import again.
Inter-site traffic on this tunnel is above the range VCF Operations learned for it. Check whether a migration, a backup or a replication job explains it before looking for a loop or a misrouted flow.

Open the object in the Global Manager and read the realization status for this location. Check the location alarms and the connection between the Global Manager and the location, then save the object again if needed.
